    Produced by Natrx with the North Carolina Coastal Federation  ·  8 min read

    Everyone knows North Carolina's coast is eroding. But how much? And where?

    The people of eastern North Carolina can point to where their shorelines used to be. Most of that shoreline is marsh, the low grassy edge of the bays and rivers, and it is losing ground. How much, and exactly where, was a best guess, assembled by inspecting one site at a time, wherever somebody could get to.

    So the North Carolina Coastal Federation went looking for a way to see all of it at once, and found one close to home. Natrx, a coastal resilience firm based in Raleigh, spent about a year working through ten years of aerial and satellite imagery and produced a rate of loss for 2,900 miles of shoreline, including long stretches no one could reach on foot. Most of that coast is giving way slowly. A concentrated part of it is going fast, and that part accounts for almost half of everything lost.

    What is lost

    What goes when the marsh goes

    Jacob Boyd is 42 and has lived in eastern North Carolina his whole life. He runs the salt marsh program at the North Carolina Coastal Federation, which means his job is finding the places where the state's money will do the most good holding a shoreline in place.

    Like most people who live on this coast, he does not need a dataset to tell him it is moving. He has watched it change with his own eyes. What he points to first is the ghost forests, stands of dead trees killed from below by salt water pushing inland.

    You can see the transitioning literally happening. Some of these ghost forests are now barely even sticks, and you can see the marsh migrating through it. Just in my lifetime.
    Jacob Boyd · Salt Marsh Program Director, North Carolina Coastal Federation
    A ghost forest of dead trees on the North Carolina coast.

    Behind those trunks, marsh moves in. In front of them, marsh turns into open water. The whole system slides in one direction.

    What is lost in that slide is not only ground. Marsh is where young fish and crabs mature. It filters the runoff coming off the land before that water reaches the bays. It takes the energy out of a storm surge before the surge reaches a road or a house. When marsh becomes open water, what is left is bottom habitat, which is still habitat, but it does almost none of that work.

    Seeing all of that was never the difficult part. Proving it was. Grant money and permits go to projects that can show evidence, and evidence means measurements. Everywhere along this coast needs work, which is another way of saying there is no obvious place to start.

    Whether they live on the coast or not, this is affecting everybody in North Carolina. It affects insurance rates, it affects everything.
    Jacob Boyd · Salt Marsh Program Director, North Carolina Coastal Federation
    What can be done

    There are ways to hold a shoreline. None of them are free.

    Erosion is not untreatable. A shoreline can be armored against the water, or it can be rebuilt to absorb what is hitting it. The options run from breakwaters set out in the shallows to living shorelines, which combine engineered structure with natural habitat so that oysters, marsh grass and trapped sediment do part of the work and the protection grows stronger as it establishes. Both have improved a great deal in the past decade as the materials and the modeling behind them have gotten better. Natrx works on this side of the problem as well, manufacturing custom-built modules sized to the conditions of a particular site rather than to a standard.

    A thriving living shoreline and the shoreline it's protecting, several seasons after installation.

    None of it is free. Each project is real, physical construction work in open water, paid for out of grants that can only be awarded once and spent once. The Coastal Federation cannot build along 2,900 miles of shoreline. Nobody can. So the whole job comes down to choosing which stretches, in what order, and on what evidence.

    The finding

    The loss is not spread evenly

    Natrx measured about 93,000 spots along those 2,900 miles. Each spot is a fixed point on land with a line running from it out to the water's edge. Measure that line in five different years and the shoreline's movement at that spot becomes a rate, in feet per year.

    Half of those spots are pulling back faster than eight and a half inches a year. Four in ten are losing more than a foot. Now rank every eroding spot from fastest to slowest and look at only the worst tenth of them.

    43.44%

    Nearly half of all the land lost came from one tenth of the shoreline measured.

    Measured across 76,052 eroding points, 2012 to 2022.

    At the worst single spot measured, the marsh edge pulled back about 46 feet in one year. Dare County, which takes in much of the Outer Banks, is the hardest hit overall. Hyde County, on the mainland to the southwest, is close behind.

    90% of the eroding coast is losing ground slowly. The other 10% accounts for almost half of the loss. That is the most useful thing in the measurement. Spread a fixed budget evenly along 2,900 miles and most of it goes to protecting shoreline that was barely moving. Pinpoint the worst spots and the budget goes where it's most needed.

    How it was measured

    A job nobody could do by walking

    Measuring 2,900 miles of shoreline across ten years of photographs, finely enough to catch a marsh edge moving two feet in a year, is not work a person can do with a magnifier and a light table. It is not a question of effort. There is simply too much of it, and much of this coast cannot be reached on foot at all.

    Sorting an enormous number of images the same way every time is exactly what machine learning is good at. Natrx built its analysis system, , around that, and trained it on established coastal science, so what the models are taught to recognize as a retreating marsh edge comes from people who have spent their careers looking at them.

    The work runs in two passes, and the reason is that the coast is not a simple line. It's a maze of creeks, bays and marsh islands. Measuring all of that precisely is slow and expensive, so the first pass is wide and quick, and the second is run only where more precision warrants the additional cost. The models sort satellite images of the whole region into marsh and not marsh, in two different years, and subtract one from the other. It covers everything fast. It does not tell you how fast any one place is moving.

    The second is narrow and exact. In aerial photographs from five years between 2012 and 2022, the models trace lines out to the edge of the marsh grass, and the change in that edge becomes a rate.

    Try it yourself

    Run the two passes in order.

    Choose a step

    North Carolina has about 2,900 miles of shoreline along its sounds, bays and rivers. Nobody can measure all of it by hand. The method starts by narrowing the search.

    The first pass is not a prediction and Natrx does not present it as one. Measured against the precise work it lines up only loosely, accounting for less than four percent of why one shoreline retreats faster than another. What it does is narrow the search, by saying which stretches are worth the expensive look. That is the difference between working from whatever somebody happened to observe recently and seeing the whole picture, including the parts nobody has ever visited.

    Where the imagery was poor, and sometimes it was, since a photograph taken at high tide does not show the same edge as one taken at low tide, analysts flagged those areas and carried them forward with lower confidence. They are also the areas where the two passes agree least, which is what you would expect.

    The methodology is public. The photographs are free. The hard part is running the same process 39 times without it drifting.
    Nick Brady · Chief Technology Officer, Natrx

    Resolution is the other reason this works. The Coastal Federation needed to catch places losing as little as two feet a year. Over a decade that is about twenty feet. In the publicly available satellite imagery, twenty feet is smaller than a single pixel, so the change never appears at all.

    Nick Brady, Natrx's chief technology officer, is matter of fact about which part of this was hard. The underlying science is published, the aerial photographs are free from a federal survey, and the machine learning is well understood. What is hard is running the same process across 39 separate areas without it drifting, and having people who can look at an ambiguous photograph of a tidal flat and say whether that is marsh or water.

    Brady estimates that doing this the traditional way would have cost several million dollars, and that even then it would not have been able to cover this much coast. A crew measuring a shoreline on foot can get through the shoreline of about one town. This project covered 2,900 miles. The Natrx analysis came to about one percent of the grant, leaving the rest for the restoration work itself.

    What changes

    Better measurements mean smaller, more focused projects

    Go back to the choice. How much structure a site needs depends on how much wave energy is actually reaching it and how fast the shore there is giving way. Without measurements the safe assumption is the worst case, and the safe design is the largest one the permit allows.

    With them, the structure gets matched to the site. Less material, fewer trucks, lower cost, and often better protection, because something built to the real conditions outperforms something built to a permit ceiling. Natrx works to the same standard on the construction side, with modules sized to what the analysis calls for rather than to a default.

    Construction of a custom engineered living shoreline.
    There are some sites where historically people have just built up to what the permit would say, even though it may not actually call for that.
    Jacob Boyd · Salt Marsh Program Director, North Carolina Coastal Federation

    Building to the ceiling is the habit, and habits move slowly. As Boyd puts it, people are used to doing things the way they are used to doing them.

    The analysis does two more things that have nothing to do with engineering. Grant money is competitive, and Boyd says a proposal with hard data behind it beats one without, which is frequently the whole difference between funded and not funded. And permit reviewers want to see evidence, so bringing it up front moves an application along faster than arguing for it after the fact.

    What happens now

    Six hundred acres, and a permit application

    The Coastal Federation is taking the ranked shoreline into early permitting conversations with state and federal agencies. Boyd expects permit applications within about six months and construction inside two years. The program aims to protect up to 600 acres of marsh.

    The funding behind all of this was awarded for exactly those acres. In 2024 the Environmental Protection Agency awarded $421 million to a four-state conservation coalition covering North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia and Maryland, and the Coastal Federation's share is roughly $30 million over five years. The purpose of that grant is keeping carbon in the ground. Marsh soil holds it, and marsh that erodes into open water lets it go.

    Interest is not confined to North Carolina. Boyd says a regional network of agencies, academics and restoration practitioners across the South Atlantic has been waiting on the results. The method needs marsh, since it reads the line of grass as the shoreline, and most of the unhardened shoreline in the Southeast is exactly that.

    Boyd has watched this happen his whole life, and watched how people have had to come around to it. After Hurricane Florence in 2018, he says, a lot of his neighbors stopped arguing about whether the coast was changing and started asking what could be done about it.

    The datasets and the mapping tools go public on the Federation's website this fall. Anyone will be able to look up their own stretch of shoreline.

    Now we have the shorelines prioritized. That's step one done for a lot of the project areas.
    Jacob Boyd · Salt Marsh Program Director, North Carolina Coastal Federation

    Plain-language definitions for the terms that travel through this piece.

    Natrx Assess
    The analysis system Natrx built for this kind of work. It reads satellite and aerial imagery to find where marsh is turning into water, then measures how fast a shoreline is moving, at one meter. The models are trained on established coastal science rather than on imagery alone.
    Marsh
    Low, salty grassland at the edge of the bays and rivers. It floods and drains with the tide and it holds the shoreline together.
    Ghost forest
    A stand of dead trees killed by salt water pushing inland, with marsh moving in around them.
    Living shoreline
    Engineered structure and natural habitat built together just offshore, so wave energy is absorbed before it reaches the marsh and the protection strengthens as oysters and grass establish.
    Breakwater
    A structure set out in the shallows to break waves before they reach the shore.
    Erosion rate
    How far a shoreline pulls back in a year, in feet. One foot a year means ten feet of land gone in a decade.
    One meter resolution
    Fine enough to see a shoreline move twenty feet across a decade. Freely available satellite imagery is not.
